title: Food, drinks and ordering
objectives: I can order food and drinks politely in a padaria, a lanchonete and a restaurant.
I can say what I like, what I want and what I prefer.
I can use the present tense of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs and explain what each ending shows.
I can ask for more, less or a little of something.
I can explain why the food words are spelled and accented as they are, using the rules for c, g, qu, ç, nasal vowels and stress.
I can tell the literal words of an expression such as pois não from what it means and how it is used.
I can talk about meals and ask for the bill.

vocabulary.note: The accent is there because the word is stressed on the third to last syllable, car-DÁ-pi-o (the ending io counts as two syllables, i and o), and a stress that far back is always marked. The á is open, like the a in father, and the final o is said u. In Portugal people say ementa.

The same word means a bank account, and it is related to the verb contar, to count. At the table it is the bill, which American English calls the check. The n ends the syllable con-, so the o is a nasal vowel: the n only nasalizes the o and is not said as a consonant.

ç is [s] before o, and om at the end of a word is a nasal vowel, so the word is said gar-SÕ with the lips never closing. The stress is on the last syllable, the default for any ending outside the a, e, o, am, em, ens group (om, like im and um), so no accent is needed. Feminine: a garçonete. To call a waiter, many people say moço or moça, a young man or a young woman (ç is [s] before o and a).
Said pa-da-RI-a. The stress is on the i, so the word needs no accent, like tia. More than a bakery: a padaria serves coffee, sandwiches and breakfast at a counter, and sells basic groceries.

ch is [ʃ], as in shoe. The a is nasal because n ends the first syllable, and the final te is said [tʃi], so the word sounds like lan-sho-NE-chee. It is built on lanche, a light meal or snack, which Portuguese borrowed from the English word lunch. A casual place with sandwiches, snacks, juices and coffee.
qui is [ki], because qu before i writes a k sound and the u is silent. At a restaurante por quilo you serve yourself from a buffet, put your plate on a scale and pay for its weight.

example.target: O restaurante por quilo é bom.
example.source_literal: The restaurant by kilo is good.

vocabulary.note: Often shortened to PF, said pê-efe. feito has the diphthong ei [ej], and it is a form of the verb fazer, to make or do, used here like an adjective: a plate already made up. A standard lunch plate with rice, beans, a meat or fish and salad at a fixed price.

example.source: I would like a set meal.

vocabulary.note: pão is the stressed nasal ending ão, and ch is [ʃ]. na is em + a, in the or on the, the contraction from the grammar-map lesson; a chapa is a hot metal plate. A French-style roll cut open, buttered and pressed on that plate. A padaria classic.

example.target: Eu queria um pão na chapa.
example.source: I would like a buttered toasted roll.
example.source_literal: I wanted a bread on-the griddle.

vocabulary.note: queijo is said [ˈkejʒu]: qu before e is [k] with a silent u, ei is a diphthong and j is [ʒ]. de is said [dʒi]. Small, chewy cheese rolls that originate in Minas Gerais. The plural is pães de queijo.

example.target: Eu gosto de pão de queijo.
example.source_literal: I like of bread of cheese.

vocabulary.note: café has an acute accent because it is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for an ending in e, and the é is open. In leite the ei is a diphthong, and the t before the final e (said i) becomes [tʃ]: LAY-chee.

-zinho is a diminutive, an ending that makes a word little or affectionate. The stress moves onto it, ca-fe-ZI-nho, so café loses its accent: the new stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in o. nh is [ɲ], like ny in canyon. In practice it is the small, strong, sweet coffee served everywhere in Brazil.

example.source: Do you want a small coffee?

vocabulary.note: rr is the strong [h] sound. z at the end of a word is [s] or [ʃ] depending on the region, like final s. The word ends in z, so the default stress is on the last syllable, ar-ROZ, and no accent is needed. Rice and beans, arroz e feijão, is the daily base of a Brazilian lunch.

ei is a diphthong, j is [ʒ] and ão is the stressed nasal ending: fei-JÃO. The singular names the food as a whole where English says beans. The plural feijões is the ão becoming ões, as in the lesson on plurals. In Brazil it usually means black or brown beans cooked in a soup-like sauce.
Carne alone usually means beef. The r ends the first syllable, where its sound depends on the region, and the final e is said i.
In fr the r follows another consonant in the same syllable, so it is a tap. The a is nasal before n, and g is hard [g] before o: FRÃ-gu.
x after ei is [ʃ]: PAY-shee. The final e is said i.
The a is nasal before n and j is [ʒ]: la-RÃ-ja. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in a.

example.target: O suco de laranja é bom.
example.source_literal: The juice of orange is good.

vocabulary.note: The Brazilian word. In Portugal people say sumo. c before o is [k].
The acute accent is there because the stress is on the first of three syllables, á-gu-a, the third to last, which is always marked. gu before a is [gw]: AH-gwa. The á is open.
c before e is [s] and j is [ʒ]. The r ends the first syllable. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in a: ser-VE-ja.
g before e is soft [ʒ], the r after f is a tap, the a is nasal before n and the final te is [tʃi]: re-fri-zhe-RÃ-chee.

ç is [s] before u. The stress is on the second to last syllable, but a word ending in r defaults to the last syllable, so the stressed vowel takes an accent. The u has only one quality, so the acute only marks stress: a-SÚ-car.

da is de + a, of the. In manhã, nh is [ɲ] and the final ã is the stressed nasal vowel: the tilde alone marks both the nasal sound and the stress. The Brazilian word. In Portugal people say pequeno-almoço.

example.target: O café da manhã é às sete.
example.source_literal: The coffee of-the morning is at-the seven.

vocabulary.note: l at the end of a syllable is [w], so the word is aw-MO-su. ç is [s] before o.
Also a verb, jantar, to have dinner. j is [ʒ] and the a is nasal before n.
Regular, with the stem com-.
Regular, with the stem beb-.
Regular except in one form: você quer, not quere. qu before e is [k] and the u is silent.
Always followed by de, so the thing liked is introduced by of. It is related to the noun gosto, taste. Before an article de fuses with it: gosto do café, gosto da salada.
The eu form changes the stem vowel from e to i: eu prefiro, not eu prefero. The other forms keep the e: prefere, preferem.
g stays hard [g] before a and o: pago, paga. Portuguese pays the bill directly, pagar a conta, with no word for for.
ou is a diphthong [ow], often said as a plain closed o: POH-ku. c before o is [k]. Used before nouns you do not count one by one, such as rice or sugar.
ai is a diphthong, like English eye. mais never changes for gender or number.
Also means fewer. It never changes for gender or number.
The opposite of com, with. em at the end of a word is a nasal vowel [ẽj̃], said like sayn through the nose, and the m does not close the lips.

example.target: Um suco sem açúcar, por favor.

vocabulary.note: ou is the diphthong [ow], often reduced to a plain closed o in speech. It has no accent. Do not confuse it with o, the, which is said u.

example.source: Do you want coffee or juice?

vocabulary.note: queria is a form of querer in a past tense called the imperfect, which the course teaches at the elementary level. For now learn it as a fixed polite formula. A past form for a wish that is present makes the request less direct, as English does with I was wondering if. It is softer than eu quero.

example.target: Eu queria um café, por favor.
example.source: I would like a coffee, please.

vocabulary.note: An informal formula for ordering at a counter. vê is the form of the verb ver, to see, used for você, and me is an object pronoun, a pronoun for the person who receives or is affected by an action, here me or for me. Colloquial Brazilian puts it before the verb. vê is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it always takes an accent, and the circumflex shows the closed e.

example.target: Me vê um pão de queijo.
example.source_literal: Me sees a bread of cheese.

vocabulary.note: Said by the person serving you, to ask what you want. pois is a linking word, roughly well or then. It is an idiom: despite the não it is not a refusal. The same words can also answer a request, with the sense of of course. oi is a diphthong and the final s is [s] or [ʃ] by region.

example.source: Good morning! How can I help you?

vocabulary.note: Said to people who are about to eat. t before i and t before the final e (said i) are both [tʃ], so it sounds like bom a-pe-CHEE-chee.

só is a stressed one-syllable word ending in o, so it takes the acute, and the o is open. isso has ss between vowels, which is [s]: EE-su. isso means that, a neutral word taught earlier. At a counter Só isso? asks whether that is everything.

alguma means some or any, and it takes the feminine form because coisa, thing, is a feminine noun. In coisa the oi is a diphthong and a single s between vowels is [z]: COY-za. Staff say it after you have ordered.
todo means all or whole, and todo dia is the everyday expression for every day. d before the i of dia is [dʒ]: JEE-a. Some people say todos os dias.
An adjective, so it agrees with its noun: caro with a masculine noun and cara with a feminine one, such as a conta. As with English dear, it can also mean beloved.

tá is the spoken short form of está, he, she or it is, with the first syllable dropped. It keeps an acute accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a. bom has a nasal vowel, so the m does not close the lips.

dialogues.title: Breakfast at the padaria
dialogues.context: Ricardo stops at a padaria on his way to work and orders breakfast at the counter.

lines.speaker: Ricardo

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.target: Só isso?

lines.speaker: Ricardo

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.target: Tá bom. Mais alguma coisa?

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.target: Só isso. Ah, e sem açúcar no café, por favor.

lines.source_literal: A bread on-the griddle, a coffee with milk without sugar and a bread of cheese. All correct?

lines.speaker: Simone

lines.speaker: Ricardo

dialogues.title: Lunch at a restaurante por quilo
dialogues.context: Camila and André have lunch together at a restaurant where you pay by the weight of your plate.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: André, você gosta de feijão?
lines.source: André, do you like beans?
lines.source_literal: André, you like of bean?

lines.speaker: André
lines.target: Gosto, sim! Eu como arroz e feijão todo dia.
lines.source: Yes, I do! I eat rice and beans every day.
lines.source_literal: I-like, yes! I eat rice and bean all day.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: E você prefere carne ou frango?
lines.source: And do you prefer beef or chicken?
lines.source_literal: And you prefer meat or chicken?

lines.speaker: André
lines.target: Prefiro frango. Eu não como carne.
lines.source: I prefer chicken. I do not eat beef.
lines.source_literal: I-prefer chicken. I not eat meat.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: Você quer salada?
lines.source: Do you want salad?
lines.source_literal: You want salad?

lines.speaker: André
lines.target: Quero um pouco de salada e mais arroz.

lines.source_literal: I-want a little of salad and more rice.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.target: E para beber? Você quer suco?
lines.source: And to drink? Do you want juice?
lines.source_literal: And for to-drink? You want juice?

lines.speaker: André
lines.target: Quero, sim. Suco de laranja. E você?

lines.source_literal: I-want, yes. Juice of orange. And you?

lines.speaker: Camila

lines.speaker: André

lines.speaker: Camila

lines.speaker: Paulo

lines.speaker: Clara

lines.speaker: Tiago

lines.speaker: Clara

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.target: Muito bem. O que vocês querem beber?

lines.speaker: Tiago

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the letters and accents in the food words
grammar.explanation:
The words in this lesson contain no new rules, only the rules of the first three lessons applied to new words. If you can see why each word is spelled as it is, you can read and spell hundreds of other words without memorizing them. For any word, ask three questions in order. Which letters are special: c, g, qu, ç, j, x, ch, nh, rr, ss, a vowel followed by m or n, a tilde? How does the word end, because the final letters decide how the last vowel sounds and which syllable is stressed by default? And does the actual stress match that default? If it does, no accent is written. If it does not, an accent goes on the stressed vowel. (A few accents are not predicted by the default, such as the one that tells pôde from pode; none of them occurs in this lesson.)

Some sounds are chosen by the letter that follows. The letters c and g are hard before a, o and u and soft before e and i. So the c of cerveja is [s] because e follows, the g of refrigerante is [ʒ] (the s of English measure) because e follows, and the g of frango, pagar and gostar stays hard because a or o follows. To write a hard sound before e or i, Portuguese adds a silent u: queijo, quilo, querer and queria all begin with [k], and the u is not said. Inside a word, [s] before a, o or u cannot be written with c, which would read [k], so Portuguese uses ç, the c with a cedilla: garçom, almoço, açúcar. (ç never stands before e or i, where c is already [s], and never at the start of a word, where s does the job, as in salada.) The sound [ʒ] can be written j before any vowel, which is why cerveja, laranja, feijão and queijo use j; g writes it only before e or i, as in refrigerante, and since g before a, o or u is hard, j is the only choice there.

Pairs of letters and position also decide sounds. ch is [ʃ], as in lanchonete and chapa. nh is [ɲ], the ny of canyon, as in cafezinho and manhã. x after ei is [ʃ], so peixe is PAY-shee. A double rr is the strong [h], as in arroz. A single s between two vowels is [z], as in coisa, and a double ss is the way to write [s] between vowels, as in isso. An l that ends a syllable is [w], so almoço is aw-MO-su. Final unstressed vowels are weak (a is uh, o is u, e is i), and a t or d before that i is said [tʃ] or [dʒ]: leite is LAY-chee, apetite is a-pe-CHEE-chee, restaurante and refrigerante end in -chee, and de is said jee, as in pão de queijo.

A vowel followed by m or n that ends its syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not said as a consonant. That is why conta is KÕ-ta, frango is FRÃ-gu and laranja is la-RÃ-ja; why garçom ends in a nasal o with the lips never closing; and why sem and bom are said through the nose. The tilde does the same job on ã and õ, and ão is the stressed nasal ending of pão, feijão and the plural feijões. In manhã the tilde on the last syllable marks both the nasal sound and the stress.

Now the accents, using the default from the lesson on stress. Words ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words ending in anything else (i, u, is, us, l, r, z, im, um, om, ns, ã, ão) on the last. In the words of this lesson an accent appears only where the word breaks the default of its ending. Café ends in e, so the default would be CA-fe, but the word is said ca-FÉ, so it takes the acute, and the e is open. Açúcar ends in r, so the default is the last syllable, but it is said a-SÚ-car, so the stressed u takes an accent. Cardápio and água are stressed on the third to last syllable (the endings io and ua count as two syllables), which no ending predicts, so they are always marked. The one-syllable words só, tá, vê and é are stressed words ending in o, a or e, and these always take an accent: acute where the vowel is open or the mark is only stress (só, tá, é) and circumflex where it is closed (vê). Words that match their default carry nothing: arroz and garçom (last syllable), carne, peixe, cerveja and laranja (second to last), and pão, feijão and manhã, where the tilde alone is enough.

An accent belongs to one shape of a word. Add the diminutive -zinho to café and the stress moves to the new syllable: ca-fe-ZI-nho is stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the default for an ending in o, so the accent disappears. It is the same logic by which the accent of mês disappears in meses. Read the table as a set of worked applications of these rules.

rows: c before e is [s]; j is always [ʒ]; the stress is the default for final a: ser-VE-ja
g before e is [ʒ]; r after f is a tap; an is nasal; final te is [tʃi]
g is hard [g] before a and o; the a of frango is nasal
qu writes [k] before e or i, and the u is silent; ei in queijo is a diphthong
ç is [s] before o and u; garçom ends in a nasal o said without closing the lips
an l that ends a syllable is [w]: aw-MO-su
ch is [ʃ]; an is nasal; final te is [tʃi]: lan-sho-NE-chee
rr is the strong [h]; final z is [s] or [ʃ] by region; z gives a last-syllable default, so no accent
nh is [ɲ], like ny in canyon; z between vowels is [z]
a single s between vowels is [z], ss is [s]: COY-za, EE-su
the nasal ending ão or ã defaults to the last syllable, so the tilde alone is enough
stress on the last syllable of a word in e breaks the default; open e, so acute
the stress moved to zi, the second to last syllable, which is the default for o
stress on the second to last syllable breaks the default for r; u takes the acute
stress on the third to last syllable is always marked; the á is open
stressed one-syllable words ending in o, a or e always take an accent; vê has a closed e, so circumflex
t before i or a final e is [tʃ] and d is [dʒ]: LAY-chee, and de is said jee
m or n after a vowel
m or n closing a syllable nasalizes the vowel and is not said as a consonant
ou is a diphthong [ow], often said as a plain closed o; c before o is hard [k]

examples.source_literal: I eat rice, bean and fish in-the lunch.

grammar.title: The present tense: what a verb ending does
grammar.explanation:
A verb is the word that says what someone does or what happens. In English the verb hardly changes: I eat, you eat, we eat, they eat, and only he eats differs. English therefore relies on the pronoun to say who is acting. Portuguese does the opposite. The ending of the verb carries that information, so each person gets its own ending and the pronoun becomes optional. This is the most important idea about Portuguese verbs, and the rest of this note applies it.

Three terms from the grammar-map lesson are needed. The infinitive is the dictionary form, which ends in -ar, -er or -ir; these endings sort verbs into three families. The stem is what remains when the ending is removed: com- from comer, beb- from beber, abr- from abrir. To conjugate a verb in the present tense is to add to the stem the ending for the subject. The present tense is used for habits and facts (Eu como arroz e feijão todo dia), for what is true now, and often for a decision taken on the spot: Eu pago a conta can mean I will pay the bill. The form for what is happening at this very moment, the progressive, comes later in the course.

The endings follow a logic, not a list. Each is a vowel that names the family (a for -ar, e for -er, i for -ir) together with a marker for the person. The eu form is the stem plus -o in all three families: falo, como, abro. In the form for você, ele, ela and a gente the family vowel stands alone, and since -er and -ir verbs both use e, only -ar verbs differ: fala, come, abre. In the nós form the marker is -mos after the family vowel: falamos, comemos, abrimos, the only slot where -er and -ir differ, e against i. In the form for vocês, eles and elas the marker is -m after the vowel: -am for -ar verbs and -em for -er and -ir verbs. That -m is the nasal ending from the alphabet lesson: -am is said like ão, weakly and without stress, and -em like ayn through the nose. English marks the plural on nouns but not on verbs, which is why a plural ending on the verb is new to you.

Stress explains why none of these forms needs an accent. In eu, você and eles forms the stress falls on the stem, which is the second to last syllable of a word ending in o, e, em or am, exactly the default: CO-mo, CO-me, CO-mem, FA-lam. In the nós form the stress is on the family vowel, again the second to last syllable of a word ending in s: co-ME-mos. The stem keeps its spelling, so the sound rules of the alphabet lesson keep working: pagar gives pago and pagam, with the g hard before o and a.

Because the eu and nós forms are unique, the pronoun is dropped freely: Como arroz todo dia. The form for você, ele, ela and a gente is shared (come can be you, he, she or we eat), so the pronoun is kept unless the context makes the subject clear. A gente takes the third person singular because it is literally the people, a third person noun: A gente come na padaria.

Negation shows the contrast with English most clearly. English needs the helper verb do to make a negative, and the helper takes the ending: I do not eat, she does not eat. Portuguese puts não before the verb and changes nothing else: Eu não como carne, Ela não come carne. The verb keeps exactly the ending it has in a positive sentence. A few verbs break the pattern; the ones in this lesson are querer and preferir, explained in the next note.

grammar.title: Wanting, liking and preferring: querer, preferir, gostar de and eu queria
grammar.explanation:
Three verbs express what you want: querer (to want), preferir (to prefer) and gostar de (to like). Each has one feature that English does not prepare you for, and they are the verbs you use to order food, so each is explained here from its logic.

Querer is regular except in one form. Its stem is quer- and it takes the regular -er endings: eu quero, nós queremos, vocês querem. Only the form for você, ele, ela and a gente breaks the pattern: the regular form would be quere, but the word is quer. Eu quero is regular, although many courses list it as irregular. The qu is the rule from the alphabet lesson again: before e the u is silent.

Preferir has the stem prefer- and the regular -ir endings, with one change: in the eu form the stem vowel e becomes i, so eu prefiro, not eu prefero. The other forms keep the e: você prefere, nós preferimos, eles preferem. Several other -ir verbs behave the same way (servir gives eu sirvo, repetir gives eu repito). It is a sound change from an earlier stage of the language, so it is learned as a pattern, not derived.

Gostar is a regular -ar verb (gosto, gosta, gostamos, gostam), and its difficulty is structural. English like takes a direct object, the thing the verb acts on with nothing between the verb and the thing: I like coffee. Portuguese gostar needs the preposition de before the thing liked, so the literal structure is I like of coffee: Eu gosto de café. Gosto café is wrong. Querer and preferir work as in English, with no preposition: quero café, prefiro frango. Because de is a preposition, it fuses with an article when there is one, as the grammar-map lesson showed: gosto do café da padaria, gosto da salada. With no article de stays whole: Gosto de café means coffee in general, while Gosto do café da padaria means that particular coffee. After gostar de you can use an infinitive: Gosto de comer peixe, literally I like of to-eat fish. Querer and preferir take the infinitive directly: Quero comer, Prefiro beber.

Politeness works through the verb form. Eu quero says I want plainly. In shops and restaurants Brazilians usually say eu queria. Queria is the eu form of querer in the imperfect, a past tense taught at the elementary level, so for now it is best learned as a fixed formula. Its logic is this: speaking about a present wish with a past form moves the wish one step away from the listener and softens the request, much as English says I was wondering if or I wanted to ask. The literal meaning is I wanted, the natural translation is I would like, and the use is a polite order. Eu quero um café, por favor is not rude, especially with por favor, and you will hear it in casual places, but queria is the safe choice with someone you do not know.

At a counter you will often say Me vê um pão de queijo. Vê is the form of the verb ver, to see, used for você, and me is an object pronoun. A subject pronoun (eu, você) says who acts, while an object pronoun says who receives or is affected by the action; me means me, or to me and for me. Colloquial Brazilian puts the object pronoun before the verb. The literal words are me sees a cheese bread, the natural translation is give me a cheese bread, and the use is an informal, friendly way to order at a counter, less formal than eu queria. The circumflex on vê is the one-syllable rule from the lesson on accents: a stressed one-syllable word ending in e is always marked, and the circumflex shows the closed e.

Staff use fixed formulas, and the literal words differ from what English says. Pois não? is may I help you?, literally well no, and not a refusal. Só isso? is is that all?, literally only that. Mais alguma coisa? is anything else?, literally more some thing. Learn each formula whole, and keep its literal words apart from its natural meaning.

grammar.title: Questions and short answers
grammar.explanation:
English builds a question with a helper verb, do (an auxiliary verb is a verb that helps another verb), and a changed word order: Do you like beans? Portuguese has no do and does not change the order. A yes or no question is the statement said with rising intonation and written with a question mark: Você gosta de feijão? is literally you like of beans? Nothing in the words marks it as a question except the voice. The tag né, a shortened não é (literally not is?), turns a statement into a request for agreement, like English right? or isn't it?: A aula é às dez, né?

The answer follows from the same logic. English short answers use the helper again (Yes, I do), but Portuguese has no helper to repeat, so it repeats the main verb. The verb changes person, because the question is addressed to você and the answer is about eu: Você gosta de feijão? Gosto. Você quer um cafezinho? Quero. If the question is to vocês, the answer is in the nós form: Vocês comem carne? Comemos. Adding sim gives emphasis or warmth: Quero, sim. A bare sim is understood but sounds curt.

In a negative answer não comes before the verb, as always. The first não answers the question and the second negates the verb: Não, não gosto. A polite refusal of an offer is Não, obrigado from a man and Não, obrigada from a woman, because the ending agrees with the speaker, as in the greetings lesson.

A choice question joins the options with ou, or: Você prefere carne ou frango? Answer with the verb and the choice, or with the choice alone: Prefiro frango. Question words from the lesson on ser and estar go first, and the rest keeps statement order: O que você quer? Quem paga a conta? Onde é o restaurante?

E para beber? is a short question in which the verb is left out because the situation supplies it (what do you want). Para here means for, and it is followed by an infinitive. After a preposition Portuguese uses the infinitive, where English often uses a form in -ing (for drinking) or to drink. Literally the phrase is and for to-drink?

When you listen, the ending tells you who is being asked: Você quer suco? asks one person, and Vocês querem suco? asks several. The answer can drop the pronoun: Queremos.

grammar.title: Quantities and combinations: um pouco de, mais, menos, com, sem, de and só
grammar.explanation:
To order you must say how much, and Portuguese uses short quantity words that never change form. Um pouco de means a little and is followed by a mass noun, a noun for something you do not count one by one, such as arroz, açúcar or salada. A count noun is counted: um pão, dois pães. De links the quantity to the thing, so the literal structure is a little of rice. Mais (more) and menos (less) go directly before the noun and, unlike adjectives, do not agree with it in gender or number: mais arroz, mais pães, menos açúcar. Menos covers both English less and fewer. To say one more, put mais before the number one, which does agree with the noun: mais um café, mais uma cerveja, literally more one coffee.

Com (with) and sem (without) are prepositions which, unlike de and em, do not fuse with articles, so the noun follows directly: café com leite, café sem açúcar. English with and without work the same way, so these are easy. What differs is how Portuguese combines two nouns. English puts the describing noun first: orange juice, cheese bread. Portuguese, which puts adjectives after the noun, puts the main noun first and attaches the other with de: suco de laranja (juice of orange), pão de queijo (bread of cheese), café da manhã (coffee of the morning). De says what something is made of, flavored with or belongs to, and com says what accompanies it. Compare pão de queijo, a bread with cheese baked into it, and pão com queijo, bread with a slice of cheese.

Só means only or just. Só a conta, por favor is just the bill, please, and Só isso? is literally only that?, meaning is that all. The accent on só is the one-syllable rule: a stressed one-syllable word ending in o always takes it.

The names of meals usually take the definite article: o café da manhã, o almoço, o jantar. With a preposition the article fuses: no almoço is em + o, and in o café da manhã the da is de + a. Eu como pão no café da manhã is I eat bread at breakfast, literally in-the coffee of-the morning. Brazilians usually have a light breakfast, a main lunch and a lighter dinner, with a small afternoon snack called lanche da tarde.

culture.title: Eating and drinking in Brazil
culture.text:
The Brazilian day is organized around three meals. Breakfast, o café da manhã, is light: coffee with milk, bread with butter or cheese, pão na chapa, often a piece of fruit, and on weekends pão de queijo. Lunch, o almoço, is the main meal and usually eaten around noon or one. Many Brazilians eat arroz e feijão every day, with meat or chicken, a salad and something fried or baked. Dinner is lighter and sometimes just a sandwich or a soup.

For a quick, cheap lunch, many people go to a restaurante por quilo, where you fill your plate from a buffet and pay for its weight, or order a prato feito, abbreviated to PF, which gives you a complete plate at a fixed price. In a padaria you can have coffee and bread at the counter at any time of day, and in a lanchonete you order juices, sandwiches and snacks like pastel, coxinha and pão de queijo.

Coffee is everywhere. A cafezinho is offered in offices, shops and homes, and refusing is possible but a little unusual. Popular drinks include fresh suco, guaraná, which is a sweet soft drink made from an Amazonian fruit, and água de coco, literally water of coconut. In restaurants a service charge of about ten percent is usually added to the bill. To ask for the bill, say A conta, por favor, or catch the waiter's eye and make a writing gesture in the air. Before eating, people say bom apetite, and for a toast they say saúde.

exercises.prompt: How do you politely order a coffee from a stranger?
choices: Eu queria um café, por favor.
Eu quere um café, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Eu queria is the polite formula: a past form used for a present wish softens the request. Querer is an infinitive, which cannot follow eu here, and quere is not a form of querer.

exercises.prompt: A waiter says 'Pois não?' Its literal words are 'well no'. What does he mean?
choices: How can I help you? It is not a refusal.
No, we do not have that.
exercises.explanation: The literal words and the meaning differ: pois não is an idiom used to invite your order. Keep the literal gloss and the usage separate.

exercises.prompt: Why is the c of cerveja said [s]?
choices: It comes before e, and c is soft before e and i.
It is the first letter of the word.
The j later in the word softens it.
exercises.explanation: c is hard before a, o and u and soft before e and i. The j of cerveja is a separate sound, [ʒ].

exercises.prompt: Why does queijo begin with qu and not with c?
choices: A c before e would be [s], so qu is used to write [k] there, with a silent u.
Because qu is the only way to write [k].
Because Portuguese never writes c before e.
exercises.explanation: To write a hard [k] before e or i, Portuguese uses qu with a silent u. The letter c writes [k] before a, o and u, so qu is not the only way.

exercises.prompt: Why does café carry an accent while cafezinho does not?
choices: The é of café becomes a tilde.
In cafezinho the stress moves to zi, the second to last syllable, which is the default for an ending in o.
exercises.explanation: An accent belongs to one shape of a word. In café the stress on the last syllable breaks the default for e; in cafezinho the stress is on zi, where the default for o puts it, so no mark is needed.

exercises.prompt: Why does açúcar carry an accent?
choices: It is stressed on the last syllable.
It is stressed on the third to last syllable.
It is stressed on the second to last syllable, but words ending in r default to the last.
The ç requires an accent on the next vowel.
exercises.explanation: a-SÚ-car breaks the default for an ending in r (the last syllable), so the stressed vowel is marked. The ç only shows that c is [s] before u.

exercises.prompt: Which syllable of cerveja is stressed, and why does the word need no accent?
choices: The last, ja, because j ends the word.
The second to last, VE, which is the default for a word ending in a.
The first, cer, because every word is stressed on its first syllable.
The second to last, VE, but an accent is forgotten in writing.
exercises.explanation: ser-VE-ja ends in a, and the default for a, e and o endings is the second to last syllable. The word matches its default, so nothing is written.

exercises.prompt: Why does arroz carry no accent although it is stressed on the last syllable?
choices: Because the default for an ending in z is already the last syllable, so the word does not break it.
Because words of two syllables never take accents.
Because z is not a vowel.
exercises.explanation: An accent is written only when a word breaks the default of its ending. Words in z default to the last syllable, and ar-ROZ follows that.

exercises.prompt: Which letter writes the sound [ʒ] before the vowel a, as in laranja?
exercises.explanation: g before a is hard [g], as in frango, and ç writes [s]. Before a, o and u only j writes [ʒ]; before e and i either j or g can.

exercises.prompt: How is the final m of garçom pronounced?
choices: With closed lips, like the m of English room.
It is not a consonant: it nasalizes the o, and the lips stay open.
It is silent and the o is oral.
As an n followed by a vowel.
exercises.explanation: An m or n that closes a syllable only nasalizes the vowel before it, as in bom and sim.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: Gostar needs the preposition de before the thing liked. English like takes the object directly, but Portuguese gostar does not.

exercises.prompt: Which is the literal, word-for-word rendering of Eu gosto de café?
exercises.explanation: The natural English drops the preposition, but Portuguese gostar requires de, so the literal words are I like of coffee.

exercises.prompt: Why does vê carry a circumflex?
choices: It is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it is always marked, and the e is closed.
It is stressed on the third to last syllable.
The circumflex makes the vowel nasal.
exercises.explanation: A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o always takes an accent. The acute marks an open vowel and the circumflex a closed one, and the e of vê is closed.

exercises.prompt: How do you say one more coffee when ordering?
exercises.explanation: Mais goes before the noun phrase, so one more is literally more one, and um agrees with the masculine noun café.

exercises.prompt: Which form of querer breaks the regular pattern in the present?
exercises.explanation: Only the você, ele, ela and a gente form is irregular: quer instead of quere. Eu quero is regular.

exercises.prompt: Which of these verbs changes its stem vowel from e to i in the eu form?
exercises.explanation: Preferir gives eu prefiro, not eu prefero. Comer, beber and abrir keep their stems: como, bebo, abro.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks 'Você gosta de peixe?' What is the most natural way to say yes?
exercises.explanation: Portuguese has no helper verb to repeat, as English does with 'I do', so it repeats the main verb, changed from the você form of the question to the eu form.

exercises.prompt: Why does Portuguese say 'suco de laranja' where English says 'orange juice'?
choices: Portuguese puts the main noun first and attaches the other noun with de.
Portuguese reverses the order of every pair of words.
exercises.explanation: The main noun comes first and de links the noun that says what it is made of: juice of orange, bread of cheese, coffee of the morning.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'pão de queijo' and 'pão com queijo'?
choices: Pão de queijo is a bread made with cheese baked in; pão com queijo is bread accompanied by cheese.
Pão com queijo is the plural of pão de queijo.
Pão de queijo is made in Minas Gerais and pão com queijo is not.
exercises.explanation: De says what something is made of or flavored with; com says what accompanies it.
An -er verb: the stem com- plus -o for eu.
The nós form adds -mos after the family vowel: com- + -emos.
Pagar is an -ar verb, and the form for eles ends in -am.
Vocês takes the eles form, and the ending for -er verbs there is -em: com- + -em.
A gente means we but takes the third person singular, the same form as você: beb- + -e.
The subject a padaria takes the shared você, ele, ela form; -ir verbs use -e.
In the eu form of preferir the stem vowel changes from e to i: prefiro.
Gostar is a regular -ar verb, so the eu form is gosto, and it is followed by de.

exercises.prompt_target: O café ___ manhã é às sete.
exercises.explanation: De + a fuse into da, because manhã is feminine and takes the article a.

exercises.hint_source: I would like a coffee, please.
exercises.explanation: Queria is the polite formula for ordering; quero would mean I want.
Sem means without, the opposite of com.

There is no helper verb do; the order is the statement order, and gostar needs de.

answers: Me vê a conta, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Both forms are natural; me vê is the informal counter formula.
Não goes directly before the verb, and the verb keeps its usual ending.
